newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire says offensive has begun, town recaptured.
newsitem.headline: Zaire says offensive has begun, town recaptured.

text.p: Zaire's government said on Thursday that its army had launched its promised counter-offensive against rebels in the east and recaptured the town of Walikale.
A defence ministry statement said that the town had fallen on Wednesday and that 100 rebels including an unnamed rebel chief had been killed. Zairean casualties were 20 soldiers wounded, it added.
Walikale is about 100 km (60 miles) north west of Goma, one of four major towns captured by the Tutsi-led rebels along Zaire's eastern border with Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda.
Rebels said in December Walikale had fallen to them but there was never any independent confirmation from journalists or aid workers.
Thursday's statement announced "the recapture of the city of Walikale by the Zairean armed forces" and accused the rebels of using drugged youngsters as human shields.
"The Zairean armed forces in effect unleashed their counter-offensive on Monday January 20 to recover (lost) national territory," it said.
Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo told the nation on Monday that in agreement with absent President Mobutu Sese Seko he had formally ordered the army to launch the counter offensive.
Thursday's statement was the first official word that the offensive had actually begun on the ground.

"This counter-offensive, which is total and devastating, intensified on January 22 with fierce fighting around Walikale, killing 100 of the enemy including a big leader," the statement said. It did not name the leader.

The Tutsi-led rebels seized towns and territory in the east after launching an offensive in October, humiliating the Zairean army which retreated in disarray. They accused Zaire of denying them citizenship and seeking to return them to Rwanda, from where their forebears migrated several generations ago.

The offensive put to flight hundreds of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees who fled to Zaire fearing reprisals after the 1994 genocide by Hutu hardliners in Rwanda of up to one million minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
Tutsi rebels seized power in Rwanda and dominate the government there. A Tutsi army controls neighbour Burundi.
Zaire accused both countries of supporting the rebels and sending troops to fight alongside them -- a charge it repeated in Thursday's statement.

Mobutu, who had been away in Europe since August when he had cancer surgery in Switzerland, returned home in December and reshuffled the government and army leadership to organise the recapture of all lost territory.
Mobutu, who seized power in 1965, has since returned to Europe for further tests.
He ruled virtually unchallened until 1990 when domestic and foreign pressure forced him to embark on democratic reforms.

Zaire's sometimes turbulent democratic transition has dragged on. National elections must be held by July under the transitional constitution but the government says lost territory must be recaptured first.
Former colonial power Belgium has urged Zaire to consider a peaceful solution to the revolt. Zaire's main opposition has also called for negotiations with rebel leader Laurent Kabila.
